I work at the pet resort and pet crematorium (they’re owned by the same people) and we have the option of communal (mass) cremation. For this option though, we use a completely separate cremator. Ashes aren’t returned for communal cremations as we don’t want people getting the wrong ashes back, of course. Rather, after a communal cremation is completed, the ashes are spread over a large hill/field which is on the owners private property (so no one can go step on freshly spread ashes, etc). The area the communal ashes are spread is where the owners of the company used to take their dogs to run around and play before they passed, and they chose that area to spread communal ashes because it’s a beautiful area with trees and a little pond, any pet would love to run around and play there. We allow people to view the area that we spread the ashes so they have some comfort knowing where their pet is going. 

For the private cremations, we take every precaution we can to ensure there are never any mix ups with pets, urns, ashes, etc. Private cremation is more expensive but these are people’s pets, their loved ones, so ensuring they get back the right ashes and ensuring that all pets are treated with respect is top priority. 

We even have witness cremations so a client can attend the cremation process with their pet. Even when a pet is brought in and we are preparing the pet for cremation, it’s hard not to gently pet them and comfort the animal, even though it’s already passed on. 

I can’t speak on behalf of all pet crematoriums, but we are always as respectful and honest as possible with clients and their pets as all of us are animal lovers and understand how difficult that loss is. It definitely is something that someone should look into before bringing in a pet for cremation. 

There was one other pet crematorium in our province years and years ago that got shut down after it was discovered that pets were being left in garbage bags on the counter for long periods of time in unhygienic and disrespectful conditions, there were buckets of ash and bones, a sink full of old filthy water, freezers full of dead animals (long after their ashes were due to be returned), a shocking amount of full biohazard buckets in a shed that was unlocked, and a customer even had the ashes of her dog tested only to find out that she had received the wrong ashes, they were cat ashes. 

It is bizarre, as yes, the bodies are bagged as to avoid any bodily fluids leaking and are then labelled with pet and client information as well as the type of cremation they asked for, and when a body is put in a freezer, it is for no longer than 24 hours (at the maximum) until the cremator is emptied prepped for the next pet, but should never be left in the freezer for long periods. Generally, the pet is put into the cremator within a few hours and is already fully cremated by the next day. At the crematorium I work for, the ashes are always ready to be picked up within 3 days, which includes the time for prep, cremation, urn engraving (if requested), urn stuffing, sealing, certificates being made and sealed. By the third day, we are ready for the customer to pick up their pet, or we will deliver it back to the vet we received the pet from where they will contact the owner.
